title: UNIT 3: SOLVING EQUATIONS
notes: ✓ Equation → a mathematical statement showing that two expressions have equal values.

title: 3.1 LINEAR EQUATION IN ONE VARIABLE
notes:
✓ Linear equation in one variable → an equation whose variable has power 1.

✓ General form → ax + b = 0, where a ≠ 0.

Examples → 10x = 20, 3x + 6 = 0, 4x + 9 = −11.

◆ Solving steps:
1. Use LCM to clear fractions.
2. Simplify both sides.
3. Isolate the variable.
4. Verify the answer.

✓ Example:
3x + 6 = 15 → 3x = 9 → x = 3.

title: LINEAR EQUATIONS WITH FRACTIONS
notes:
✓ To solve equations containing fractions, multiply both sides by the LCM of the denominators.

Example:
x/2 + 3 = 7
Multiply by 2 → x + 6 = 14
✓ Therefore → x = 8.

✓ Always substitute the answer into the original equation to check it.

title: 3.2 SYSTEMS OF LINEAR EQUATIONS IN TWO VARIABLES
notes:
✓ System of linear equations → two or more linear equations considered simultaneously.

✓ Linear equation in two variables → ax + by = c, where a and b are non-zero constants.

✓ Solution → an ordered pair (x, y) that satisfies all equations simultaneously.

Example:
2x + y = 15 and 3x − y = 5.
✓ Their solution is (4, 7).

title: TYPES OF SYSTEMS
notes:
◆ Unique solution → two lines intersect at exactly one point.

◆ No solution → two lines are parallel and have different y-intercepts.

◆ Infinitely many solutions → the two equations represent the same line.

✓ The solution must satisfy both equations at the same time.

title: 3.3.1 ABSOLUTE VALUE EQUATIONS
notes:
✓ Absolute value → the distance of a number from zero on the number line; it is always non-negative.

✓ For p ≥ 0 → |x| = p means x = p or x = −p.

✓ If |x| = negative number → no solution.

Example:
|x + 2| = 6
x + 2 = 6 or x + 2 = −6
✓ x = 4 or x = −8.

Example:
✓ |x| = −1 has no solution.

title: SOLVING ABSOLUTE VALUE EQUATIONS
notes:
✓ For |ax + b| = c, first isolate the absolute value expression.

✓ If c > 0 → solve two equations:
ax + b = c
ax + b = −c.

Example:
2|2x − 1| − 1 = 5
2|2x − 1| = 6
|2x − 1| = 3
2x − 1 = 3 or 2x − 1 = −3
✓ x = 2 or x = −1.

title: 3.3.2 QUADRATIC EQUATIONS
notes:
✓ Quadratic equation → ax² + bx + c = 0, where a, b, c ∈ R and a ≠ 0.

◆ a → leading coefficient.
◆ b → coefficient of the middle term.
◆ c → constant term.

◆ Three main methods → factorization, completing the square, and quadratic formula.

title: QUADRATIC EQUATIONS BY FACTORIZATION
notes:
◆ Steps:
1. Move all terms to one side so the other side is zero.
2. Factorize.
3. Set each factor equal to zero.
4. Solve each equation.
5. Check the answers.

Example:
x² + 3x = 0
x(x + 3) = 0
x = 0 or x + 3 = 0
✓ Therefore → x = 0 or x = −3.

title: COMPLETING THE SQUARE
notes:
✓ Completing the square converts a quadratic into a perfect-square expression.

✓ For x² + bx + c, add and subtract (b/2)².

Example:
x² + 6x + 7 = 0
x² + 6x + 9 − 2 = 0
(x + 3)² = 2
x + 3 = ±√2
✓ x = −3 ± √2.

✓ This method is useful when factorization is difficult.

title: QUADRATIC FORMULA
notes:
✓ For ax² + bx + c = 0:

x = (−b ± √(b² − 4ac)) / 2a.

✓ Use the quadratic formula when the equation cannot easily be factorized.

Example:
x² − 5x + 6 = 0
x = (5 ± √(25 − 24))/2
x = (5 ± 1)/2
✓ Therefore → x = 3 or x = 2.

title: DISCRIMINANT
notes:
✓ Discriminant → D = b² − 4ac.

◆ D > 0 → two distinct real solutions.
◆ D = 0 → one repeated real solution.
◆ D < 0 → no real solution.

✓ The discriminant is found inside the square root of the quadratic formula.

title: RELATION BETWEEN ROOTS
notes:
✓ For ax² + bx + c = 0 with roots α and β:

✓ Sum of roots → α + β = −b/a.

✓ Product of roots → αβ = c/a.

Example:
x² − 5x + 6 = 0.
Sum = 5.
Product = 6.
✓ Roots → 2 and 3.

title: 3.3.3 EQUATIONS INVOLVING EXPONENTS
notes:
✓ Exponential equation → an equation in which the variable occurs in the exponent.

✓ If a > 0 and a ≠ 1, then aˣ = aʸ implies x = y.

◆ Useful laws:
aᵐ × aⁿ = aᵐ⁺ⁿ
aᵐ / aⁿ = aᵐ⁻ⁿ
(aᵐ)ⁿ = aᵐⁿ
(ab)ⁿ = aⁿbⁿ
(a/b)ⁿ = aⁿ/bⁿ
1/aⁿ = a⁻ⁿ.

Example:
2ˣ = 8 = 2³ → ✓ x = 3.

title: SOLVING EXPONENTIAL EQUATIONS
notes:
✓ Main technique → express both sides using the same base, then equate the exponents.

Example:
3ˣ = 1/27
1/27 = 3⁻³
Therefore → 3ˣ = 3⁻³
✓ So → x = −3.

Another example:
2ˣ⁺⁴ = 32 = 2⁵
x + 4 = 5 → ✓ x = 1.

title: RADICAL EQUATION EXAMPLE
notes:
Example:
√(15 − 2x) = x.

✓ The radicand requires 15 − 2x ≥ 0 and the right side requires x ≥ 0.
Thus → 0 ≤ x ≤ 15/2.

Square both sides → 15 − 2x = x².
Rearrange → x² + 2x − 15 = 0.
Factor → (x − 3)(x + 5) = 0.
Candidates → x = 3 or x = −5.

✓ Since x must be non-negative, x = 3 is the valid solution.

title: GEOMETRY APPLICATION
notes:
Example → A triangle has a base of a cm and each leg is 6 cm longer than the base. Its perimeter is 54 cm.

Equation → a + 2(a + 6) = 54.
3a + 12 = 54.
3a = 42.
✓ a = 14.

Each leg → 14 + 6 = 20 cm.

✓ Answer → sides are 14 cm, 20 cm and 20 cm.

title: AGE AND NUMBER APPLICATIONS
notes:
◆ For consecutive numbers → represent them as x and x + 1.

◆ For consecutive even numbers → x and x + 2.

◆ For consecutive odd numbers → x and x + 2.

✓ For age problems → define the present age first, then express other ages in relation to it.

Example → The sum of two consecutive numbers is 67.
x + (x + 1) = 67
2x + 1 = 67
x = 33.
✓ Numbers → 33 and 34.

notes:

✓ ax + b = 0.

◆ Linear system:
✓ ax + by = c.

◆ Quadratic equation:

◆ Quadratic formula:
✓ x = (−b ± √(b² − 4ac))/(2a).

◆ Discriminant:
✓ D = b² − 4ac.

◆ Sum of quadratic roots:
✓ α + β = −b/a.

◆ Product of quadratic roots:
✓ αβ = c/a.

◆ Absolute value:
✓ |x| = p → x = ±p for p ≥ 0.

◆ Exponential equality:
